m.c: May the Lord, your comforter, keep your heart from all fear and give you steadfastness for this day. Walk with your head held high, knowing that he fights for you. May his peace and blessing go with you at every step. Trust in him today.
h: On this day, November 24, 1572, the reformer John Knox died in Edinburgh, Scotland. He was one of the leaders of the Protestant Reformation in his country. For years he preached with great boldness and, because of his faith, did not hesitate to speak frankly to kings and queens. His ministry left a deep mark on the Church of Scotland.

His last days were days of weakness. On November 9, 1572, he installed James Lawson as his successor in St Giles’ church in Edinburgh, and went home for the last time. There, surrounded by friends and a few of the kingdom’s most important nobles, he asked that the Bible be read aloud. On the day of his death, his young wife read to him from Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians.

He was buried in the churchyard of St Giles’, and the nobles of Scotland attended his funeral. Beside the grave, James Douglas, Earl of Morton, recently appointed regent of the kingdom, spoke the words that remained in the memory of the people: “Here lies one who never feared any man.”

That sentence did not describe a man without fears, but someone who had learned that the fear of God frees us from the fear of men. Knox was not perfect, and his character was sometimes harsh. But his life teaches that the believer who rests in God can speak and act with firmness, without being overpowered by the pressure of the powerful or the opinion of the crowd. Today his memory invites us to ask God for the same firmness, to speak the truth with conviction and with respect.
m: The sentence spoken beside John Knox’s grave makes us think of how many times our decisions are guided by fear of what people will say. Isaiah asked the people: who are you, that you fear mortal man? And he reminded them that they had forgotten the LORD, their Maker.

First, identify your fear for today. Is it a difficult conversation, a meeting, a decision you have put off? Name it before God. A fear that has a name loses some of its strength. Remember that the one who comforts you is the same one who stretched out the heavens and laid the foundations of the earth.

Second, put into practice what Moses said by the sea: “Fear not, stand firm, and see the salvation of the LORD, which he will work for you today.” Standing firm does not mean doing nothing; it means trusting and obeying. Diligently do what falls to you, and leave in God’s hands what you cannot control.

Third, live with integrity. Knox read the Bible until the last day of his life. Today, before you go out, read a few verses and ask God for a word for your day. A clear conscience and a mind filled with Scripture give an assurance that no applause can give. And treat others with respect: Christian courage must always be joined to love. Walk today fearing no one, but revering God. If anyone presses you today to do something that does not please God, pray before you answer and ask for wisdom, for God gives to all generously and without reproach.
o: Almighty God, at the beginning of this day, we thank you, for you are our comforter and our refuge. You say in your Word: I, I am he who comforts you; who are you, that you fear mortal man? Today we want to believe these words with all our hearts and walk free from the fear that paralyzes.

Lord, you know the fears we carry this morning: what people will say, criticism, the uncertainty of work, health, the future of our children. We place them in your hands. As to the people by the sea, you tell us: fear not, stand firm, and see the salvation of the LORD, which he will work for you today. You fight for us, and we can be still in you.

Give us the courage to speak the truth in love and to do what is right even if it is not popular. Free us from pride and harshness, and make us at once humble, gentle, and firm. May our fear be for you alone, the beginning of wisdom. Guide our steps, protect our family, and bless the work of our hands. Walk with us this day. May your power always sustain us and your love guide us, Lord, today and always. In Jesus’ name, amen.

t.c: May the risen Lord stay with you tonight and fill your home with his peace. Give him your weariness and your worries, and sleep soundly in his arms. Tomorrow, his compassions will be new for you. May your home be a place of peace.
h: On the very day of the resurrection, two disciples were traveling from Jerusalem to a village called Emmaus, about seven miles away. They were sad and were talking about everything that had happened with Jesus: his death on the cross and the confusing reports that his tomb was empty. They had hoped that he would be the one to redeem Israel, and now they felt that all was lost.

While they were talking, Jesus himself came near and walked with them, but their eyes were kept from recognizing him. He asked them what they were discussing, and they told him of their sorrow. Then he, beginning with Moses and continuing through all the prophets, explained to them what the Scriptures said about him. He showed them that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and so enter into his glory.

As they came near the village, Jesus acted as though he were going farther. But they urged him, saying: “Stay with us, for it is toward evening and the day is now far spent.” So he went in to stay with them. And when he was at table with them, he took the bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to them. Then their eyes were opened, and they recognized him; but he vanished from their sight.

They said to each other: “Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked with us on the road and explained the Scriptures to us?” At that very hour they got up and returned to Jerusalem, to tell the other disciples what they had seen. Weariness and sadness turned into joy, for they had been with the risen Lord. That walk, which had begun in sadness, ended with a burning heart and news they could not keep silent: Jesus is alive, and he walks with his own even if we do not always see him.
m: The disciples of Emmaus made a long journey with Jesus without knowing it. Sometimes we, too, spend the day loaded down with worries without realizing that he is near. Tonight, before you sleep, is a good time to recognize him.

First, invite him to stay. The disciples did not let Jesus simply pass by; they urged him. Say to him in a simple prayer: “Stay with me tonight.” He never refuses a sincere invitation. If you are tired or sad, open your heart to him and tell him everything, as they did.

Second, let his Word set your heart on fire. What made the disciples’ hearts burn was not a spectacular miracle, but hearing the Scriptures explained by Jesus. Read a short passage tonight, slowly, and ask yourself what God is saying to you through it. A few verses read in faith can comfort you more than many hours of anxiety.

Third, rest and believe that God renews your strength. Isaiah says that those who hope in the LORD will renew their strength, they will soar on wings like eagles, they will run and not grow weary. Today you did what you could; the rest belongs to the Lord. And tomorrow, when you get up, do as the disciples did: tell someone what God has done in your life. Sleep in peace, for Jesus stays with you. Take a pause tonight, breathe deeply, and repeat in your heart: Lord, you are here. That certainty is enough for you to rest and begin again tomorrow with hope.
o: Lord Jesus, at the fall of evening, we say to you, like the disciples of Emmaus: stay with us, for it is toward evening and the day is far spent. Thank you for walking at our side throughout this day, even if at times we did not recognize you. Thank you, because your Word made our hearts burn and because you come in to stay with those who invite you.

We thank you for the strength you gave us today, for the work accomplished, for the people we met, and for the bread we shared. Forgive us the sadness and doubt with which we sometimes walk along the road, as if you were far away. Open our eyes to see you at the table, in the Bible, and in the faces of our brothers and sisters.

Tonight we give you our weariness. You give strength to the weary and increase the power of the one who has no might. Renew our energies for tomorrow and, for those who hope in you, make them rise up on wings like eagles. Take care of our families, comfort the afflicted, and give rest to those who suffer. We lie down in peace, for you, Lord, make us dwell in safety. Thank you for your faithfulness, Lord. In Jesus’ name, amen.
